geo_headlines: HOUTHI ATTACK ON RIYADH AIRPORT KILLS 12. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said 12 people were killed and 309 injured in a Houthi attack on King Khalid airport; the Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response, and Trump said he would "take a look" at joining strikes on the Houthis (Al Jazeera). **This is the main new risk for oil when futures reopen at 6 PM ET tonight; Brent settled Friday at $104.72, just under the $105 trigger.**

US JET DISABLED A BLOCKADE RUNNER. On Saturday the US military said a fighter jet struck the stern of the cargo ship Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman after it left an Iranian port and ignored warnings; the crew was unharmed. Hormuz transits fell to the lowest in more than two months (Reuters). Putin relayed Iran's position on a peace deal to Trump in a Friday call (AFP).

ISAIAS: FOUR DEAD, GULF OUTPUT STILL SHUT. At least four deaths were linked to the storm (AP). About 670,000 customers were still without power midday Saturday, and 69% of Gulf oil output and 57% of gas output remained shut; Shell and Chevron began returning crews, and the Energy Department authorized up to 4 million barrels of reserve oil exchanges (Reuters via Digg).

FRIDAY RECAP: S&P 500 0.09% BELOW TUESDAY'S RECORD. S&P 500 7,811.54 (+0.59%; +1.15% on the week), Dow +0.83% (+0.93% week), Nasdaq 100 +0.51% (+0.24% week). Sunday re-check: Friday's highs are unchanged, so the no-record finding stands. 10-year 5.24%, 2-year 4.80%. VIX 14.84. Bitcoin $82,922 (+0.01%).

THE WEEK AHEAD: CPI AND BANKS. Mon: bond market closed for Columbus Day; stocks open. Tue: JPMorgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo, Citi, J&J and UnitedHealth. Wed 8:30 AM: September CPI, consensus 3.6% from 3.4% (core 2.5% from 2.4%); Bank of America and Morgan Stanley. Thu 8:30 AM: retail sales, PPI; TSMC. Fri: options expiration (Live Trading News).
client_frame_short: The weekend added one new risk: a Houthi attack on Riyadh's airport killed 12, and Trump said he would look at joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis. **Oil is the market to watch when futures reopen tonight, because Brent settled Friday at $104.72, right at our $105 trigger.** Stocks ended a good week less than a tenth of a percent below Tuesday's record, and this week's tests are inflation on Wednesday and the big banks starting Tuesday. Expect headlines to stay noisy; for clients, the plan does not change, and no portfolio moves are needed.
client_frame:
If a client calls this weekend, the story is a strong week for stocks with one new Middle East risk heading into Monday.

What happened: a Houthi attack on Riyadh's main airport killed 12 people and injured 309. The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response, and Trump said he would "take a look" at joining strikes on the Houthis. Separately, a US jet disabled a cargo ship trying to run the Iran blockade, and fewer ships are moving through Hormuz. Trump has said he won't strike Iran itself before the November 3 midterms, but the conflict around it is widening, not calming.

Oil: Brent settled Friday at $104.72. Hurricane Isaias still has about 69% of Gulf output shut, though crews are returning. Energy is where these risks show up first, and higher fuel costs already pushed Delta to cut its 2026 forecast on Friday.

Stocks: the S&P 500 gained 1.15% last week and finished 0.09% below Tuesday's record, even after Thursday's AI scare.

This week: September CPI on Wednesday, with consensus expecting headline inflation to rise to 3.6% while core stays near 2.5%. That gap shows the inflation problem is mostly energy, which matters for the Fed's October 28 decision. The big banks report Tuesday and Wednesday and will give an early read on how consumers and companies are holding up.

Why it matters: a balanced portfolio is built to absorb exactly this kind of weekend news. Trying to trade around headlines usually costs more than it saves, and history rewards staying invested through stretches like this.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds pay more than 5% for a decade, and long-term equity plans do not need changing. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (now 5.24%), a 30-year above 5.75% (now 5.60%), or wider US military action that keeps Brent well above $105 (Friday $104.72).
